To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we provide a tight bound on the sample complexity of a class of quadratic classifiers that depends on the level of isotropization of the data distribution, (ii) this bound improves the dependence on dimension of the best previously known result, (iii) this dependence on the level of data isotropy is also present in other models, such as neural networks, and (iv) the dependence on the covariance matrix is similar in the two models, which is not a coincidence

(i) we provide a new bound on the Radamacher Complexity of quadratic classifiers, which depends only on the intrinsic dimension and the largest eigenvalue; (ii) the new bound improves on the best previous bound; (iii) we demonstrate that the bound is tight in the isotropic case; (iv) we provide empirical evidence that the bound is also tight for non-isotropic distributions; (v) the new bound is tight even for non-isotropic data with a large intrinsic dimension; and
1. The Rademacher Complexity of quadratic classifiers is upper bounded by the sum of the largest eigenvalue and the intrinsic dimension of the data distribution.

the following question: How does the intrinsic dimension of the data distribution affect the sample complexity of a learning algorithm?
the following question: what is the minimal number of samples needed to learn an isotropic quadratic classifier?
the question of how the generalization performance of a quadratic classifier is affected by the intrinsic dimension of a dataset.

the sample complexity of a quadratic classifier depends only on the intrinsic dimension of the data and not on the ambient dimension, and the dependence on the intrinsic dimension can be further reduced if the distribution is isotropy.

the intrinsic dimension is the key quantity to understand the behavior of the generalization error in high-dimensional settings.
